OIL PRICING AGREEMENT-NEGOTIATIONS BETWEEN FEDERAL GOVERNMENT AND PROVINCE OF ALBERTA-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. Given the fact that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) will meet tomorrow with his Alberta counterpart to try to end the oil pricing impasse, and given that this impasse has crippled the Canadian oil exploration industry and shipped millions of dollars to foreign producers, leaving us ever more dependent on fragile sources of supply, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling):
That the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources bargain in good faith and avoid the temptation to make political points, and thereby bring sanity to the Canadian oil picture.

Their team will be lost if such an agreement is not reached or significant progress is not made. Since 50 per cent of the major equipment and bulks will come from Ontario and Quebec, and 50 per cent of the supply-erect subcontracts will come from Ontario and Quebec, with a value of some $1.6 billion and the creation of thousands of jobs, it is imperative that both sides come to an agreement quickly. That the Government of Canada quit creating jobs in Saudi Arabia, Venezuela and Mexico and start creating jobs in Canada by coming quickly to a fair and realistic agreement on energy pricing.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. Oil prices have increased 12 times since the beginning of 1980, for a total of $12.79 per barrel; 72 per cent of this $12.79 has ended up in the federal government coffers in the form of increased taxes. The Alberta proposal of July, 1980, would have resulted in a price increase of only about half this amount, or about $6.50 per barrel. So all Canadians have today are high energy taxes and low energy development.
What instructions has the government given to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources to break the deadlock with Alberta, a deadlock which has been caused directly by Liberal government greed and the broken election promises of the 1980 election?

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Solicitor General and it concerns another promise broken by the government. As the minister knows, members of the RCMP across Canada feel betrayed and double-crossed by the failure of the Liberal government to make their pay increase retroactive to January 1 this year as was promised to them last July. This breach of trust, which costs each member at least $750, has shown the minister's div-rep system to be totally inadequate.
In view of the fact that many members of the force are now actively supporting the right to no-strike collective bargaining, will the minister explain his recent threat to end contract policing? Will he also explain his union busting threat to cut the size of the force if there is any movement by mounties to form a union, a threat which his colleague, the Minister of Labour, will recognize as being an unfair labour if such a threat were made by anyone else?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, if a 22,000-man police force, working from one coast of Canada to the other, were ever to have the right to strike, or to move in the direction of having the right to strike, the possibility of such a strike and the damage it might do to the security and order of Canada would have to be taken into account by the government. The mandate of the RCMP can remain as broad as it is, it can serve the Canadian people at three levels of government, in every province and territory, precisely because the force does not have the right to strike, and the Canadian people know they can fall back on it.
In so far as the preamble to the hon. member's question is concerned, I think the force has been served very well by the div-rep system. When the recent pay raise went before Treasury Board, account was taken of the fact that the RCMP does
not have the right to collective bargaining or the right to strike. It was taken into consideration that a group within the public service which does not have that right should be compensated for its forbearance, and that was taken account of when the pay raise was settled.
I have reviewed the record very carefully, and there have been deep misunderstandings. I think these misunderstandings, well intentioned, have been on both sides, on the side of the RCMP and on the side of the Treasury Board. Since then I have had several meetings with the President of the Treasury Board, and I expect to have good news for the force very soon.

Madam Speaker, no one has ever suggested the right to strike. We are talking about the right to collective bargaining. It is the government's betrayal of its promises that will lead to the action which the minister is suggesting should not take place. His blackmail is resulting in the growth of the association of 17 divisions.

First, in the year commencing April 1, 1980, the RCMP received an increase of 12.9 per cent on payroll. That translated to between 13 per cent and 14 per cent altogether in cost. That was set forth in the estimates for 1980-1981 for the year terminating March, 1981.
Last year there was an agreement in principle with respect to a change in the year to a calendar year. Treasury Board ministers felt that with the entire package of items put before them, the RCMP was very generously treated, and that particular change was one which was not in the best interests of the government or the taxpayers of Canada.
I would point out that, for the year ended March 31, the force had received a 12.9 per cent increase in that period. In addition, Treasury board ministers had agreed to a 12.2 per cent increase for the year April 1, 1981, to March 31, 1982, which translates into more than 13 per cent. In addition to that, other measures were taken, for example, reducing by one

year the period of time it takes a first class constable to reach maximum pay.

As the hon. member for Edmonton West just pointed out, at report stage there are 135 amendments. Two of them have been debated and the votes thereon deferred. One had a short debate and was defeated on division. Two more are under debate. That leaves 130 amendments which have not been touched at all. Those 130 amendments include a few government amendments. Of course, it will want to get them through, so I suppose that is why we are getting two more days on report stage as well as one at third reading.
Before this two-hour debate is over, I am sure we shall be told, as we always are in these debates, that this is not closure, it is only time allocation. I do not know how one can avoid the use of the word "closure" when the effect of the motion is to close off debate. Also we shall be told, judging by former debates, that the government is only exercising a right found in the rule book. In other words, we will be reminded that Standing Order 75c is in the book.
I remind the House that when it was passed some 12 or 13 years ago, it was passed under closure. It is hardly a rule which represents the will of the Parliament. But granted that it is there now as a rule to which the government can resort, may I also say that there is another rule in the book which gives hon. members the right to put down motions at report stage. I believe this right was established in 1968 when we did away with the old practice of having every bill go into committee of the whole, whether or not it had been sent to a standing committee. It was felt that the committee of the whole process, especially on bills which had had standing committee treatment, was taking too long and that there should be some shortening of the total process. So we established the right to make amendments at the report stage.
In view of the fact that members might put down the same amendments, and in view of the fact that some amendments might overlap others or be out of order, we provided that the Chair was to assess the amendments put down, group them where necessary, rule them out of order if she had to, and so on. But with those conditions it was established as a rule, as a right, that members could put down report stage amendments. Members of this House have done that to the tune of 135 amendments. That is their right. Madam Speaker has assessed the amendments and she has reduced the number of possible debates to something in the order of 50. It is a little difficult to

assess her treatment exactly since in some cases whether there is to be a debate or a vote on another amendment depends on what happens to the first one. At any rate, something in the order of 40 or 50 amendments can be debated, and there can be that number of votes. Madam Speaker did a particularly Herculean job when she reduced the last 76 amendments to one, leaving 59 to be debated.
The Speaker did her duty with respect to the matter and yet this democratic right of the members of this House to debate these report stage amendments is just brushed aside, when we have dealt with only five of them, by the government using another rule which says that, so far as the 130 are concerned, boys and girls, forget it.
In my view, Mr. Speaker, Standing Order 75c is no way to run Parliament at all. Standing Order 75c applied to 130 other amendments which have not even been discussed is certainly about the most absurd thing I have seen in this House for a long time. I remind hon. members that these amendments relate to taxation, which is supposed to be a fairly important function of Parliament. I also remind hon. members that there seems to be a new principle in this bill which is before us which has not been around here before, namely, that of indexing taxation. This means that taxes can be increased without a reference back to Parliament itself. It is a pretty significant piece of legislation and yet here we have this proposal that the right accorded to us of a report stage debate, so that we can get at these various clauses and reject them or amend them as we may, is completely taken away.
The only thing the government sees is that the debate is lasting too long, as far as it is concerned, and so it falls back on 75c. To me, this is grossly unfair. It is wrong. It is an insult to Parliament and, as I have said on other occasions, every time the government uses this form of closure it simply puts off the day when we will have some sensible allocation of the time of the whole session and do our business in an orderly fashion instead of doing it at the whim of the government. This is not Parliament, to be dictated to in this way by the government. When the vote comes on this motion after this two-hour debate, we in this party will be voting unanimously and vigorously against it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, unfortunately, I cannot agree with the comments of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) even though he is a well-known authority in interpreting our Standing Orders. I maintain that the procedure which we are using, that is, the limitation of debate on this important bill, is justified. The bill which was referred from the committee with a great number of amendments has been discussed at length, and to plan the business of the House, it became necessary to use the provisions of Standing Order 75c to limit the debate. It might be useful to remind the House that there are two paragraphs in our Standing Orders, paragraphs 75a and 75b, which provide a means to avoid the situation in which we find ourselves when using Standing Order 75c.
The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) referred to some of the discussions which we have had. However, he knows quite well that these discussions provided no indication as to when we could have third reading of this bill. If we want to plan the business of the House, we must refer to paragraph A and try to come to an agreement to allot time. When that is not possible, we can use paragraph B, which provides for situations where one group of parliamentarians disagrees, and which allows such groups two hours after the motion is tabled to discuss it. Finally, when there is complete disagreement, we follow the procedure outlined in paragraph C, which we are now doing, because it is the responsibility of the government to plan the business of the House.
Are we justified in limiting debates on Bill C-57? Yes, we are, because this bill was studied at length in the standing committee following an agreement which was admittedly contrary to custom, since this review would normally have occurred in a committee of the whole, and every party in the House has found it useful, because of the nature and the complexity of the bill and the diversity of the subjects which it covers, to have it studied in a standing committee rather than in a committee of the whole. The standing committee took 23 sittings to review the bill. Many witnesses were heard, others who could not attend the sittings submitted briefs, and the Minister of Finance himself, contrary to the allegations of the hon. member for Edmonton West, appeared before the committee and explained the principles underlying the various provisions of the bill.
These discussions and this examination must be taken into account when we talk of limiting the debate since the work of a parliamentary committee is in a way an extension of the work of the House itself. At the report stage, during the first three days of debate, 37 members were recognized, namely 29 conservatives and eight New Democrats, and the hon. member for Edmonton West himself criticized the Liberals for not rising to speak. We did it precisely so that more views could be heard. Even if we were dealing specifically with amendments Nos. 1 and 3, the debate covered all the provisions in the legislation so that views divergent from those of the government were extensively stated during the debate on the first and third amendments.
On the fourth day spent on the consideration of motions we were only able to dispose of motions Nos. 1, 2 and 3 and as the two previous speakers pointed out, the bill contains 135 amendments. I agree with him that by grouping them the Chair has reduced their number to about 50. However, considering our rate of progress since the beginning of the report stage of the bill, we could easily be nearing the next budget and still be discussing the provisions or amendments to the bill under consideration.
Under the circumstances, the government decided to use the provisions of our Standing Orders, these well-known provisions of last resort I will admit, which could have been avoided had
June 9, 1981

all the parties in the House agreed on a reasonable time limit for the debate at the report stage and in third reading. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I do not think it is fair to say that this procedure is unparliamentary since it is provided for in the Standing Orders of this House. Indeed, if compliance and use of these rules are considered unparliamentary, that means that the Standing Orders themselves which govern Parliament are unparliamentary. It would be undemocratic if the official opposition had not had the opportunity to express its views on this bill. As I mentioned also, this bill has been under consideration for quite some time and not only has the official opposition been able to express its views but because of the procedure to which all parties in the House agreed, many citizens' groups were able to voice their opinion on this piece of legislation, precisely because members of this House agreed to refer this bill to a standing committee rather than to the committee of the whole.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, in the three days of debate that will follow, I will have the opportunity to explain the seven amendments proposed by the government, three of which, as members will recall, being of a purely technical nature. I will also be able to explain why indexing as used with regard to excise tax on tobacco and alcohol is justified. It is a means of taxation which is directly related to the ad valorem tax, for example, the 9 per cent tax. This tax does not come under consideration in the House every time the item or goods changes value. The revenues generated by this 9 per cent tax being directly related to the value of the item, the tax increases also. The approach used for tobacco and alcohol therefore resembles the ad valorem tax and allows the percentage of revenues derived from the excise tax on tobacco and alcohol to remain constant. As I said, Mr. Speaker, I will again have the opportunity to explain all the principles underlying the various provisions of Bill C-57 during the two-day debate at the report stage and the one day debate on third reading.

They have been betrayed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). They have been betrayed by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde). Now they have been betrayed by the House leader of the government. The same

It will not be "Non, non" from those Quebecois even though it affects all the manufacturing industries in Quebec. They will not be around.
Where are the people with the grapes in their district? Where are the Liberal members from the Niagara Peninsula? They will be there saying, "Yes, yes". They do not care what happens to the grape industry as a result of the indexing of the 9 per cent federal sales tax on the price of wines, beer and liquor. They will not be here defending the grape growers and wine producers. They will be saying, blindly, "Oui, oui-yes, yes."
I have a letter in my hand. I do not have time to deal with it in this speech but I will deal with it later. It states what the government's amendment relating to beer will do. It is a letter from the Brewers Association of Canada. There is a further increase contained in the amendment which the minister moved to this bill. The letter says, in part:
-on top of the original indexing increase, on top of the 29 per cent increase in the basic federal excise rates ... on top of the recent change in Ontario-
And so on. It says that the working man will no longer be able to afford to have a beer. Where are the protectors of the working men in the ranks opposite? They will be here burping out, "Yes, yes, aye, aye". They will burp it out, those defenders of the beer drinkers over in the government benches.
What else is here? Where are the defenders of the universities and educational institutions? Where is the Secretary of State (Mr. Fox), who says he will now give more money for research to the universities? He will be here saying "Aye, aye", even though this bill will remove the exemption from the 9 per cent sales tax which universities have enjoyed for the last number of years when they buy equipment for research and teaching purposes. As this bill is worded, they will get very few exemptions in future. It is going to cost the universities and the post-secondary institutions millions and millions of dollars, yet the government says that it is concerned and worried about scientific research and will grant more money.
Where are the great defenders of the press? Do we see defenders of the free press on the other side of the House? All those worthy members who have small town newspapers in their constituency should be concerned because this bill contains a tax on advertising inserts in newspapers. It imposes a tax on the advertising inserts for the small weekly and monthly newspapers in the country. Surely that is an important matter. Surely it should be debated and ventilated in this House and the amendments that we have put forward should be considered.
Where are all the defenders of the people on the other side of the House? They are going to come out of their trough in a few minutes. They will hear the bell and will have to break away from whatever trough they have their noses in at the moment. They will have to come into this House and say "Oink, oink". They will have to say "Aye, aye". They will have to say "Yes" to the stampeding of Parliament, to rushing this bill through the House. They will have to say "Yes" to the gutting of Parliament. They will have to do the dirty work that the parliamentary assistants, assassins and eunuchs have asked them to do.
This is the sixth occasion so far that closure has been crammed down our throats in the House on bills of fantastic importance, such as the borrowing of something in excess of $20 billion. We have already had it once on the national gas tax legislation which is now before committee. We have had closure on the Constitution. We now have closure on this bill which is going to change the system of taxation for the cosmetic industry, which is going to change the system of taxation for the whole manufacturing industry, which is going to index taxation so that from now on taxes will automatically increase every year on beer, on alcohol and on tobacco. All that is contained in this bill, Mr. Speaker. It is an important principle: taxation without representation. That is what the people of Canada are getting from this government; they are getting taxation without representation. How can we represent the people of Canada when the government does not want the amendments that we suggested in committee to come before the House? This is an important principle. Revolutions and riots have been fought on the principle of taxation.
This is the most reprehensible incident since the Boston Tea Party. This government joined King George III, Genghis Khan and Barbarossa in the foul tactics it uses to pass taxation legislation without proper discussion or consideration.
I believe I am coming close to the end of my time as you nod in your inscrutable way, Mr. Speaker. I say to the fishermen of Newfoundland and to the Canadian people that I hope they are watching the performance today to see how the stalwart heroes they elected to form a majority government are treating them again. The government has already taxed the people 12 times. There have been 12 increases in the price of oil and gas and nine of them have been federal tax increases. There will be another tax as a result of this bill. There will also be an automatic indexing of what people pay for their beer, their glass of wine, their little drink of scotch, if they dare to have a

That would be intolerable, Mr. Speaker, and the people know it. The government was elected to govern and at some point, if agreement cannot be reached through discussion, negotiation or consensus, then it has to take its responsibility and lead. Mr. Speaker, I want to reiterate that in no way do we support this automatic indexing of taxes. Indexing of taxes is like a licence to steal. It is not a simplistic little matter of a few pennies that we are talking about. If we continue with legislation like this, it will just destroy the parliamentary system.
I want to talk about a section of the bill. I do not think the majority of Liberal members understand the bill, nor do they understand the implications of the National Energy Program. I want to refer to Clause 4 which deals with the petroleum and gas revenue energy tax. Liberals have fooled very few people about this because the message is getting out across the country. I refer to a full page advertisement which appeared in a Saturday edition of The Globe and Mail. It refers to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde). The headline reads "Do you believe this man?" In part the article reads:
Marc Lalonde is very busy these days trying to soft-sell the national energy policy being foisted on Canada. He has an unenviable job because his NEP is one of the greatest disaster scenarios of our time.
That is why we cannot rubber stamp Bill C-57. It is tied in with a disastrous National Energy Program. Hon. members on the other side do not understand what they are doing. Many Ontario Liberals should start doing some research because they are the ones who will be walloped the hardest, much worse than Albertans will be.
I have another article in my hand. Its headline reads "Fed oil policy 'will cost us 60,000 jobs' ". What on earth is the government doing, wanting to proceed with programs such as outlined in Bill C-57 and in its National Energy Program which will cost 60,000 jobs? Yet the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is going around the country telling Canadians what a wonderful bill it is. What is wonderful about losing 60,000 jobs? This article reads, in part:
More than 60,000 jobs may be lost by mid-summer due to the increasing number of oil and gas rigs leaving Canada, the Canadian Association of Oilwell Drilling Contractors warned yesterday.
Stan Jones, executive director of the association, said the 50 per cent decline in the number of rigs drilling for oil and gas during the past year has surpassed their worst predictions.
And yet we have a government with a policy that wants to pay world prices for imported oil. Why does the government want to pay world prices for oil from countries such as Venezuela, Mexico and OPEC nations when it can get oil for about half the price in Canada? Phased in over a three-year period, the Canadian price will rise to about 75 per cent of the world price. Paying Canadians would make sense; all the money would stay in Canada. Why are hon. members opposite so concerned about OPEC, Mexico and Venezuela? What is it the Liberals have against Canada?

subsubtopic: MOTION RESPECTING ALLOCATION OF TIME FOR REPORT STAGE AND THIRD READING OF BILL C-57
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
Do they know that $500,000 an hour is leaving this country to buy imported oil? We have oil in every province in Canada.
I want to tell hon. members what this disastrous policy in Bill C-57 and in the National Energy Program is doing to my province. As a result of this 8 per cent tax in Bill C-57, all oil exploration is being closed down in the province of Manitoba, just at a time when we could have had a great economic boom. A number of new discoveries have been made in Manitoba, in the Virden area and in other parts of the province. There is no way anyone will go into oil exploration or bring in rigs when the oil is sold at $17 a barrel. It is impossible to make a profit selling oil at that price. These people have to have a proper cash flow. On the other hand, there is no concern about spending $40 or $50 a barrel on oil from some Arab country, Mexico or Venezuela. It is to heck with Manitoba; do not give that province anything.
The maritimes are being affected too by Bill C-57 and the ridiculous National Energy Program. A headline in the Chronicle-Herald for May 29, 1981, reads: "Europeans cancel out on visit to Nova Scotia." the article commences:
British and European industrialists have cancelled a week-long, oil-related mission to Nova Scotia next month because of Ottawa's national energy policy.
The industrialists say the policy discriminates against foreign companies and artificially forces wellhead oil prices down to unrealistic and uneconomic levels.
The same mission has also cancelled a proposed visit to Alberta.
Here was another opportunity for more production in Canada and for working toward making the nation self-sufficient. But this government is on a program that for the next ten years will spend an additional $182 billion a year to import oil and will see us only about 55 per cent self-sufficient.
I have a document from the Wetaskiwin riding of Alberta. It is a report prepared for the Nisku Businessmen's Association. It contains statistics and names of firms that will be affected by Bill C-57 and this ridiculous National Energy Program. In Alberta, 77 industries are cutting back on any expansion and are laying people off. And I tell members from Ontario, that 55 eastern Canadian industries are named. I suggest that members on the other side get a copy of this document, and if they cannot get a copy they can contact me and I will see that one is sent to them. Companies in Alberta and in eastern Canada are listed. There are probably some companies from ridings of members opposite. Hon. members should look them over and see how their ridings are being affected.
In this excellent document on page 20 we read:
It is an economic principle that when one section of Canada's economy is affected by some event, other areas are also directly affected. This can be seen in the cutbacks in orders to suppliers from the oil and oil related firms in the Nisku Industrial Park. The Federal Budget and NEP have caused slowdowns and loss of sales in these firms, which in turn decreases their expenditures on supplies and inventories.
Through our survey we obtained a list of suppliers in Alberta and Eastern Canada who have been affected by the decrease in spending.
This means more layoffs and cutbacks. Why do we need a program like that? We certainly hope that the two energy ministers reach a conclusion tomorrow. I hope the federal
June 9, 1981

minister will see the light when he meets with the Alberta energy minister tomorrow and that an agreement is reached so as to get production going in Canada. The government should get its mind off OPEC, Venezuela and Mexico. We should be concentrating on the Canadian oil industry and jobs here, never mind worrying about all these other countries and sending billions of dollars to them.
On page 22 of this report prepared for the Nisku Businessmen's Association, we read:
As a result of cutbacks or cancellations of purchases by the 41 companies responding to our survey, $1,470,000 in revenues was lost by Eastern suppliers in the last quarter of 1980.
The article continues, but I see that my time is up. I hope Ontario members will open their eyes and for starters get hold of this document.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am an Ontario member and I have certainly had my eyes opened this afternoon. I have seen the conduct of members opposite and I have listened to their ridiculous comments. As a member who comes from the province of Ontario, I have no hesitation or compunction in supporting Bill C-57; nor do I have any hesitation or compunction in supporting this motion to allocate time for further stages of debate and third reading.
As pointed out by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), we have used this quite legitimate device to end debate, a device called for in the rules of the House of Commons, a number of times this session. I think the public of Canada wants an efficient government and they want an efficient Parliament. They do not want to see an opposition, which has had its full opportunities to make its views known on a particular measure, continue debate and essentially prevent the government from getting on with the affairs of governing the nation.
Some members opposite have talked about closure. We are not talking about closure this afternoon, we are talking about time allocation. The hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) when he was House leader in 1979 used this very rule on Bill C-20, the mortgage tax bill. He referred to it as a fair and gentle measure. Any responsible government that wants to get its legislation program through in the face of hostility and filibustering on the part of the opposition must have some means at its disposal to get on with legislation and the governing of the nation. That is what we are engaged in this afternoon.
Time allocation is a legitimate rule. It is used at Westminster. In fact, I was just reading some of the debate which took place previously during this session on this very point. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has made a couple of good speeches on the matter, one of which I think was on January 13 of this year. He made eminent sense when he said-I am paraphrasing him so I hope I am not too inaccurate-he would like to sit down with the government at the beginning of each session and map out a parliamentary time-
Time Allocation
table. The government wants to change the rules of the House of Commons to make it more efficient, but there is no way we can get our friends on the Conservative benches to ever come to some agreement so we can have organization of the business of this nation.

Obviously the hon. member does not know his colleagues. That is another example of the wild generalizations we get from the other side. They make allegations unsubstantiated by fact.
In any event, on the whole question of parliamentary reform, I am sure the government would welcome means by which we could legitimately organize the legislative time in the House of Commons as is done in Great Britain, where second reading debates very rarely go beyond two days, with some routine bills being sent to a second reading committee. I am sure the government would be amenable to discussions, but certainly with the attitude we have had expressed by the Conservative party in the official opposition, that will be difficult. Members of the official opposition really want to complain at every turn and are not interested in seeing that this country is governed properly or that good legislation comes forward. So what can we do but use the legitimate rules at our disposal?
The House leader of the official opposition, the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker), was quoted in a CP wire story yesterday, when talking in terms of the proposed foreign affairs debate-I am sure you will remember this during question period yesterday, Mr. Speaker-as saying that there seems to be a two-day debate on foreign affairs anyway and the Conservatives would rather spend their opposition days debating economic problems. So here we have it with the official opposition wanting an economic debate, yet what are they going to do this coming Thursday when they have an opportunity through an opposition motion to debate economic issues? That party will be bringing forward a mischievous motion dealing with capital punishment, a motion that is going to embarrass their leader and party members more than it will embarrass anybody on this side of the House. This is a party that wants to talk about economic issues, but when it has the opportunity to do so it does not.
I think we are quite justified in using 75c on this bill because the official opposition has shown in the days this bill was under discussion in the House that hon. members opposite are not really interested in talking about the 135 motions on the order paper. What did we have? For two straight days we had a whole litany of grievances and allegations against the government. We did not have a good, specific debate on the amendments before us. Without being too gratuitous, Mr. Speaker, it was you and your colleagues in the Speaker's chair

June 9, 1981
Time Allocation
who rightly called the debate to order and said: "Just a minute, this is the report stage debate on certain amendments and remarks must be directed to those amendments". That is called for in our rules and it is backed up by precedents in Erskine May's and Beauchesne's. We have an official opposition that really is not interested in discussing specifics.
This afternoon the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) did not really talk about the specific amendments. Did he talk about specific clauses during the debate in the House? Perhaps he has not participated in the debate, but all the interventions he has made on general economic subjects, whether during opposition days or during question period, have been very short on specifics but very long on innuendo, throwing charges across the floor and making political gain. He and his colleagues are not interested in a legitimate economic debate.
We have before us an official opposition that does not really know what it wants from this Parliament. It is an opposition that has not really decided its own position on many economic questions facing our time, whether they be energy or taxation questions. We have heard two, three or four different versions of party policy. Each time a member makes a speech it seems he says things which are at odds with official opposition party policy. We have seen this during the question period and we have seen it during this debate. The official opposition falls back to making generalized, second reading type speeches at report stage, forcing the Speaker to direct hon. members on that side to speak specifically to the clauses of the bill.
I hope at some point in the next year we can discuss parliamentary reform and, as has been suggested by members on both sides of the House, organize our parliamentary timetable so we can have meaningful debate and this place can become efficient. Until that time and until we streamline Parliament-and we must streamline Parliament or become increasingly irrelevant to the Canadian public-the government has every right and obligation, and would really not be discharging its duty otherwise, to use the legitimate rules in the Standing Orders of the House of Commons to move debate forward.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, in listening to the comments by members on the other side, I think you should perhaps question whether they are really interested in talking about economic matters, whether they are really interested in legislation going through, or whether the official opposition understands its role in Parliament, which is to criticize and propose alternatives, but not to filibuster and prolong debate, and not to force governments into using these rules.
We would like to deal with the business of the House in a more co-operative and conciliatory manner. I think we have shown during the whole debate on the Constitution how parties can come together when there is a real desire. I implore members of the official opposition to stop this continual barracking, this continual blocking of Parliament, and to work with the government in trying to address the affairs of Canada in order to improve economic policy in this country; and, yes, to criticize where justified rather than continually criticizing
and blocking every legitimate attempt to try to give good government to this country.

subsubtopic: MOTION RESPECTING ALLOCATION OF TIME FOR REPORT STAGE AND THIRD READING OF BILL C-57
speechtext:
As hon. members know, Mr. Speaker, we are under a very strict time limit here with a closure motion involving, in effect, a two-hour debate and members having to contribute what they have to contribute in a period of ten minutes. We will then have the vote. Therefore, it is not really possible for members to reply to all points or really to discuss all the matters for debate in Bill C-57, when debate is being cut off at the pass.
I am not going to get into a personality debate here, but I have sat and listened to the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Evans), and to the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Col-lenette) particularly, speak so piously about the business of the House, suggesting we should reform procedures and adopt rules that will make this business of Parliament efficient so the Canadian public will get its dollars' worth. Yet the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council did not have the guts to say, as he knows full well, that he as the parliamentary secretary having something to do with the order of the business of this House, has not yet even structured the Committee on Procedure and Organization to review the archaic procedures of this House and decide what rules should be changed. He has an incredulous look on his face. We have not yet structured a basic committee. I have been waiting since this Parliament was convened to see changes in some of the rules in this House. There have not even been meetings, and the hon. member talks about reform of the House!
I have been here along enough to know that, regardless of what rules there are in the rule book, without good faith and respect among members of Parliament on both sides, being human as we are, hon. members can pervert or prostitute any rule. There must be good faith and respect. We cannot build good faith with misleading statements. Perhaps the statements to which I refer were not deliberately intended to mislead the audience which looks into this chamber from time to time and tries to figure out what goes on. There is a duty on officials of this House, and on parliamentary secretaries especially, to make sure that when they speak, they state the truth. They should not keep talking inside out when they talk about the truth. The Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council talks about this opposition not being concerned about the business of this country.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: MOTION RESPECTING ALLOCATION OF TIME FOR REPORT STAGE AND THIRD READING OF BILL C-57
speechtext: That is true.

subsubtopic: MOTION RESPECTING ALLOCATION OF TIME FOR REPORT STAGE AND THIRD READING OF BILL C-57
speechtext:
Did the hon. member read the motion put forward by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) yesterday? That motion was seconded by the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker), my House leader, and it reads as follows:
That this House condemns the government for again unnecessarily raising petroleum taxes and thereby burdening all consumers, but particularly consum-
June 9, 1981

ers of heating oil, with prices far in excess of those promised without providing relief to those hardest hit and least able to adjust.
What did we do with that motion yesterday? We debated it all day, as the parliamentary secretary knows. But then he did a very dishonest thing. He told the truth inside out, and that is what gets my Irish dander up. Hon. members talk about a filibuster. We are not arguing about the rules of the House just now. There is a motion allocating time, but the government in effect is using the bludgeon of closure, and that determines the atmosphere and the level of respect in this institution.
In the few minutes I have left, and without getting into the guts of this bill, I will come to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance, who was not quite so extreme with his misinformation. However, how can the opposition be blamed for the incompetence of the government House leader in arranging government business? Hon. members opposite cannot have it both ways. They have brought forward an omnibus bill to which there are 135 amendments. If we reduce it to a structure on which the House can vote, there are, in effect, 35 amendments. It will take eight hours if we vote on all of them, and we certainly could. Hon. members opposite cannot have it both ways. Either they have a bill or they have several bills.
I agree with the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance that Bill C-57 is fantastic in scope. It is one of the two legs of the whole National Energy Program, considering the excise taxes which are involved. The government should be precise with its bills. If it was precise, this House could have definable debates on specific issues. We could have votes without getting into crazy, self-serving, Catch-22 situations in which the government blames us for protesting when it brings in closure.
Let us talk about closure. This bill is fundamentally a tax bill. To the radio audience, the television audience and the public taxpayer, this bill establishes a precedent. I do not want to get into an argument with the hon. member for Ottawa Centre, but this bill establishes a precedent. If we index excise taxes to the cost of living, the amount compounds and keeps increasing as the cost of living increases. The government has an interest in seeing the cost of living go up because taxes will then go up. If we index excise taxes, why not index the personal income tax? We have indexing at the bottom end to help those caught in the inflationary squeeze. They can deduct the index factor from their taxes. Shall we apply this principle at the top? If we have this principle for the excise tax, should it be applied to the income tax or the corporate tax?
Many years ago the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) uttered the sentiment that members of Parliament are nobodies. Perhaps that sentiment will be borne out. Through modern technology tax increases might be directly defined by the cost of living, and members of Parliament and 23 million or 24 million Canadians-whatever number is determined after the census-can all sit in their homes and push little computer buttons so that the House of Commons will not even have to meet.
Time Allocation
You know the history, Mr. Speaker. I am afraid some of our parliamentary secretaries do not know the history of Parliament. The purpose of Parliament is to control the public purse. That is the reason the first Parliament met 1,000 years ago, but that matter could involve a whole speech.
Let me deal with the alleged filibuster about which the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council speaks. No one has yet mentioned that this whole matter was referred to a committee because of an agreement among members of this House. On Thursday, February 12, there was an order of the House that on Friday, February 13, 1981, all questions respecting the second reading stage would be put at the end of the day and the matter referred directly to the committee. At second reading of a bill there is usually an opportunity for hon. members to ventilate some of the principles of the bill. That right in this case was removed by agreement. The agreement was made on the expectation that the bill would go to committee and that important people would come before the committee, as they did, to submit their briefs. That was done and most of the briefs expressed protest. Out of that committee came 135 amendments. Now we do not have a chance to have a real debate at this stage. That opportunity is being taken away from us.
It will be a month of Sundays or perhaps four years down the road before I will again agree to such a proposition, because we were hoodwinked. What has been demonstrated today by the government House leader is a type of parliamentary larceny. We spent one day at second reading. Perhaps we were too amenable when we entered into the agreement. This important bill went to committee. The government was urging us to get on with it, but the committee was not called until March 19. It was referred at second reading on February 13. The committee was not called until March 19 and, under the terms of the House order, the committee reported on April 16. The last committee hearing was on April 14. There were committee hearings in that month. However, if this is such an urgent, high priority item and the subject of closure today, why did the government wait since April 14, the date of the last sitting of the committee, until this stage?
We all know that at this report stage we have debated the bill on May 26, May 28, June 2 and June 4. There have been four days of debate at the report stage. We can consider a day to be four hours, or stretch it to five hours. We have had either 16 hours or 20 hours of debate at this stage.
We are talking about a tax bill which contains one of the fundamental cornerstones of the National Energy Program. We are also talking about closure. I find it absolutely incredible that on the day before the government tries to settle the energy tax problem it imposes closure on a tax bill.

speechtext: Democracy in action.

speechtext:
I heard the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) indicate-and I wish he had led his party in this particular way-that his party was specifically concerned about two items and part IV of the bill. If hon. members opposite had concentrated on that, I think we could have had a full, honest, serious and constructive debate on that particular subject. The House would have had an excellent debate limited to areas which are very important.
But what do we have? We have the opposition coming down with something in excess of 100 amendments to this bill. And I suggest, with respect, even breaking it down into 30 or 38 votes, whatever it is, that this is going to dilute the power of the debate rather than making it stronger. So if there is an abuse here, Mr. Speaker, it is the abuse of overdoing the amendments to make a point. I am not sure what all the reasons were, but it dilutes the debate. People are confused when they look at all the amendments and wonder why they are there, why they are being grouped together and why two members propose the same amendment. Why was there not agreement among the opposition? If they had things they wanted to concentrate on, why did we not hear from them on those particular subjects and not have all these amendments to the bill?
Now, Mr. Speaker, one area where I do agree with the previous speaker is that the House, in the final analysis, will only operate by agreement on all sides. The House leader and I suspect his parliamentary secretary, the House leaders of the opposition and the NDP, got together in all probability and tried to work out some method whereby we could have a full debate on this subject, where we could use Standing Order 75a and have a time allocation that all parties could agree to. But that did not take place, so 75a could not be used. Obviously Standing Order 75b could not be used because we had to go through that particular procedure in order to get to Standing Order 75c.
Mr. Speaker, 75c is a legitimate rule of Parliament and is meant to be used. And I say, with respect, that there is failure on all sides when we cannot reach agreement. But surely there comes a time when the government has to take its responsibility and move under rule 75c in order to get the business of the House through.
Now, Mr. Speaker, maybe it was not prophetic but some 11 or 12 years ago, in July of 1969, an article in the Sarnia Observer entitled "Weaker by the Week" said this:
The real threat to Parliament isn't the possible danger of cutting off productive and informative debate on a measure, but the steady erosion of prestige by tiresome speeches, lack of decorum, obstructionism and poor attendance in the House. The House of Commons is it own worst enemy and every time it aids its own weaknesses it chips away a little more of its own fabric.
The tragedy of the House of Commons, and why the press and people in the gallery leave this place, is that we bore them with long and tiresome speeches. We do not give them constructive and solid debate so that they can see there are two or three sides to an issue. With 130-odd amendments there is no question; we bore ourselves to death. So if we are doing that to ourselves, what must we be doing to the people out there? It seems to me that that editorial was bang on. When we chip away in this way, we chip away at Parliament itself.
I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, that this kind of procedure will result in the same thing that I see happening to rule 43. When I first came here some 13 years ago, rule 43 was not used the way it is today. When you rose on a matter of pressing and urgent necessity, it in fact was just that.

Then he carries that to its logical extension by saying: "We do not have to change, we do not fear what the artistic community thinks, because when election time comes around we will come up with some goodies for them which will outdo all the things we have done during our government".

On the question of advertising supplements the government has not moved. On the question of a definition of a newspaper the government has changed the tax by 5 per cent. That is the sum total of the government's move.
On the question of tax exemptions for the handicapped, again the government refused to move. On an exemption for prosthetic and other devices, the government has failed to move. On marginal manufacturing, the government has failed to move. On the concerns expressed by universities with respect to instruments used for scientific research, the government has failed to move. These are all the areas in which the

government has failed to move to any degree or in any manner of significance.
The hon. member for Sarnia is the chairman of the finance committee. 1 have a considerable amount of respect for the way in which he has handled that committee. He said that there was no agreement to restrict time. Of course there was no agreement to restrict time. The reason was because the government acted in bad faith. The government restricted debate by an agreement on second reading to send this matter to committee, but on the assumption that it would be discussed in committee and that the reasonable proposals put forward would be considered favourably by the government.
The actions of the government have run completely counter to that. I am not asking the government to abandon its points of principle. We have seen many people who have genuine complaints and problems. The government simply dismisses them by saying, "This is a special interest group". The attitude expressed by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance (Mr. Evans) is typical of the hard, bureaucratic attitude of the department. The only amendments which are coming up here are from people who have nests to feather. That is the attitude of the hon. member for Ottawa Centre toward the average Canadian taxpayer-it is just somebody who has a special beef. I think it is a disgraceful attitude for someone in politics. He should be sensitive to the concerns and the realities of business.

I know perfectly well what the hon. member said. That would have been bad enough, were it not for the final straw. Tomorrow the government will enter into discussions with the government of Alberta with respect to the national energy policy, trying to get an agreement on the questions of oil pricing and revenue sharing, and with respect to the position of the federal government vis-a-vis taxation. I find it extraordinary that, on the eve of this discussion and the discussions with Saskatchewan and British Columbia which will follow, the Liberal government would invoke closure on the petroleum and gas revenue tax.
The federal government is enacting a form of taxation which amounts to a royalty. Whether or not one agrees, one could hardly argue that it is not a direct invasion of a field of taxation which up until now has been the exclusive reserve of the provinces.

speechtext:
The government said that it is entering into these discussions in good faith and with some flexibility. The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) said in committee that
everything is negotiable and that they were prepared to negotiate as long as Alberta was prepared to negotiate. If the federal government is prepared to negotiate, why is it insisting that Parliament pass a bill by Friday which it will have to amend, if the government is in fact to reach an agreement with the province of Alberta this month or next month?
The only conclusion we can draw from the government's determination to ram through the bill is that it is not really interested in being flexible and in reaching an agreement. This is the fundamental contradiction in the position of the government. It is not simply that members of the government are not prepared to listen to those people who have come to them in good faith; they dismiss them all as special pleaders or special interest groups. It does not matter from where they come or about what they talk; they just have their nests to feather. Those are the words of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance. When it comes to a question which strikes at the very heart of the economics of confederation and the fiscal relationship between the federal government and the provinces, the government says it is prepared to be flexible. Yet on the very eve of negotiations, it insists upon forcing through this bill. Those are the two fundamental contradictions in what the government is doing.
The reason the government is closing off debate is that it is afraid to listen to the concerns of Canadians with respect to the effect of this piece of legislation. The government is afraid to enter into negotiations when it must be flexible and demonstrate its good faith. That is why the government is forcing through this legislation. It is for that reason and no other.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it would be appropriate to refer again very briefly to the provisions of Standing Orders 75a, 75b and 75c to understand what is going on now from a procedural point of view. Many members have pointed out that there were abuses of the Standing Orders in several instances; I would not want to dwell on it, everybody agrees. However, perhaps there is one Standing Order which is not unduly abused, and I refer to Standing Order 75a which provides for consultations among the representatives of each party, and for agreement to set the length of a debate on a specific bill. And if there is something which is regrettable at this time in a debate of this nature it is indeed the bad use or the non-use made of Standing Order 75A. It is available to Parliament and it was put there so that this institution can have full debates but also make a minimum of progress.
Now then, we must admit that what has happened in this instance is that a great number of days have already been allotted to the debate on Bill C-57. It is a bill to amend the Excise Act; it has to do with taxes or a form of levy which results from the budget. Everybody knows that when the budget was read in the House last fall, it was followed by a six-day debate during which we dealt with most of the questions that are the subject matter of the bill under study. To
June 9, 1981

begin with, therefore, it can be said that many members had an opportunity to comment on this bill during the budget debate which lasted six days. If we add to those six days the second reading stage, when it was agreed to refer the bill to a standing committee rather than to a committee of the whole, with that day required for second reading we have a total of seven days. Then there was the important committee stage where the clause by clause study took up another seven days. Those seven days are added to the seven others I have just mentioned so that we have had 14 days of debate on this one and only piece of legislation, Bill C-57. Let us add to those 14 days-and this is nothing more than a fact-the four days we have used up so far at the report stage and we get 18 days all told. On top of those 18 days, there will be three more which we are prepared to set aside under the terms of the motion which will be voted on later today-because the debate will not end in a few minutes, after the vote on the motion of the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Bussieres)-therefore three more days of debate on this bill plus the other 18 make a total of 21 days of debate on one single bill, not to mention the rest of the day today which will be fully allotted to the study of Bill C-57, that is this evening from 8 p.m. to 10.30 p.m. So we are indeed at 21 and a half days, that is more than 21 days of debate on one single bill. I have therefore no difficulty justifying the use of Standing Order 75c whose provisions enable the government to limit the debate when the parliamentary leaders or the party representatives fail to reach an agreement. So, to get back to the point I raised at the beginning of my remarks-

I insist this is not a misuse or non-use of Standing Order 75a. We should take more opportunities to apply Standing Order 75a in order to allow more bills to be debated in the House. On the one hand I recognized the necessity of having a full and complete debate. I just summarized in French that over 21 days will have been allowed for discussion of this bill in the House of Commons.
On the other hand, I think it would be fair and reasonable that sometimes representatives of each party come to an agreement under 75a to limit the period of time for the conclusion of debate on a specific issue. To my knowledge, this has not happened often in the past. In fact, I do not believe it has ever happened, since I became a member of Parliament in 1974, that representatives of parties in this House have come to an agreement under 75a. With the very heavy agenda which we face, I think it is about time that representatives of the parties consider this tool which is available to us, in the Standing Orders so that we can complete some business in this Parliament and can ask for the respect of the population of Canada.

Yes, that is the only time that we did it. That was an important time. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) reminds me that we did this with regard to "O Canada". I remember that occasion. We had no other choice but to do that, and we did it. We should repeat the experience; it was a useful one for this country. Why not repeat it?
May I remind you, Mr. Speaker, that on the Order Paper at this time there are still at least 35 items of legislation which must be dealt with. From now until the end of June, when this House normally breaks for the summer recess, there are only 12 government days left, including today. The rest of the days until that time are allotted to the opposition. Since we have returned from the Easter recess not one bill has been adopted by this House-not a single bill. Only the second reading stage of one bill was adopted in this House, which was the young offenders bill, after two or three days of debate. We have tried to bring forward pieces of legislation on Friday afternoons, when it is normally easier to get legislation through. We have tried to pass non-controversial legislation, yet nothing has been adopted. The opposition has seen fit to delay, to obstruct and to prevent the government from even adopting the second reading stage of bills, except for the young offenders legislation. What I am saying today, Mr. Speaker, is that the opposition should not complain too much about this government sometimes trying to place reasonable time limits on debate on some pieces of legislation.
I think the opposition also has a role to play in this House, a role to collaborate, to allow this Parliament to work. But it is not assuming its role properly. I cannot accept those who are saying that we are trying to force legislation through this institution, taking this bill as an example. On the contrary, this bill will have received more than 21 days of debate either in this House or in committee. This is only one of many bills resulting from the budget. We have tried to come to an agreement as to a reasonable additional length of time, but without success because the opposition is stunned and does not want this House to work.
We have no other choice, if we want to be responsible, but to use a means which is legally at our disposal, a means which is a Standing Order in existence in our Standing Orders under 75c. We cannot use 75c, which is limitation of time for debate, unless we have tried and unless we have given the opposition a chance to make its proposal as to an additional reasonable length of time. They have refused to negotiate properly. They have refused to agree to a reasonable length of time, which is why we have no other choice but to propose the three additional days about which I have been speaking. [Translation]
Under these circumstances, Mr. Speaker, I suggest this responsible government would be remiss if it allowed the opposition to keep on abusing the time of the House. As I said, I regret that since the Easter recess, the House has been unable to adopt a single piece of legislation. All the opposition would permit the House to do, after two days of a painful and

speechtext: Why did your House leader use it?

subsubtopic: MOTION RESPECTING ALLOCATION OF TIME FOR REPORT STAGE AND THIRD READING OF BILL C-57
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the fact of the matter is we are not a parliamentary democracy here in any real sense of the word. What we have here is a five-year dictatorship.
As the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood (Mr. Rae) pointed out, a number of very valid and legitimate recommendations by way of amendments to this bill were brought forward at committee stage. There was no movement from the government on those points. It seems to me that the rule is that once something comes out of cabinet then that is it. Once bureaucrats have placed something on the cabinet table and once cabinet has said that is it, Parliament has no right to expect any changes. It is as if we have no right to expect any modifications. We are not here to legislate, we are here to rubber stamp what the geniuses in the Privy Council office have put forward. That is our role.
The one power which we have had is the power to give speeches and try to affect public opinion, to perhaps influence public opinion in such a way that the bureaucrats will hear about it and suggest changes to the ministers in order that we might see some changes. But even that seems to be too much for this government, which suggests that it is intolerable to have members of Parliament giving speeches here trying to influence the public. The government suggests that we must have efficiency, and what efficiency means is to get in line with the rest of the sheep and rubber stamp everything which comes out of the cabinet. Parliamentary reform coming from any member of this government means to eliminate the minuscule power which we now have to give speeches in the House.
It used to be that if a minister acted arrogantly, would not negotiate, or lacked concern about representations from the opposition, you could hold up supply by holding up the estimates. That was the traditional power of Parliaments; but that was done away by closure, by the Trudeau administration.
The basic view of this group is that, once the election is over, the seats are counted and the leader of the party with the most seats selects his cabinet, that is the end of the matter. Members of Parliament have no authority, no power and no ability to legislate in a way which is in keeping with the traditions of a parliamentary system. Indeed, it is perhaps embarrassing to have to admit it, but I wonder what the heck we are doing here. It perhaps says something about our collective intelli-
June 9, 1981

gence that we are even here, because we are not legislators and we cannot do anything.
The President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) says he wants to negotiate, that he wants to work things out. If that is the case, why not let committees set their own references? Why not, in fact, have ministers negotiate with the House and let us participate in the legislative process? If there is insistence upon the finality of a cabinet decision, and that the ultimate end of any process must be a rubber stamping of what comes from cabinet, then the government has relegated us to a position where our only role is to make speeches and try to influence public opinion. But the government wants to cut that off, too. Incidentally, that is why the premiers and the provinces are as strong as they are. The people know that we cannot do anything to influence government and that we cannot be a check. Therefore, they look to the provincial governments to be a check. If hon. members are interested in making this country work, they should make this Parliament work. Then this country would work.

subsubtopic: MOTION RESPECTING ALLOCATION OF TIME FOR REPORT STAGE AND THIRD READING OF BILL C-57
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MOTION RESPECTING ALLOCATION OF TIME FOR REPORT STAGE AND THIRD READING OF BILL C-57
speechtext:
The hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood accurately pointed out the absurdity of talking about flexibility in energy policy negotiations while imposing the PGRT through closure. The petroleum and gas revenue tax has been responsible for the loss of 50,000 jobs. These are jobs in Weyburn, Saskatchewan, Brooks, Alberta, and St. John's. They are not jobs in Windsor so maybe they do not count. However, people have been put out of work. Have we had any real discussion of the PGRT here? No. It just affects western Canadians and they do not matter. The loss of 50,000 jobs does not matter.
The excise tax on natural gas has been ruled to be ultra vires by the appellate court of the province of Alberta. We are being asked to vote, through closure, on provisions which have been declared illegal by a superior court of this land. The Supreme Court will be hearing the appeal of the federal government on June 16, I understand. It may change the decision and it may not. However, as matters now stand, the provisions of Bill C-57 are illegal, and yet, through closure, we will be forced to divide on that issue and on those questions. How arrogant and how absurd-

subsubtopic: MOTION RESPECTING ALLOCATION OF TIME FOR REPORT STAGE AND THIRD READING OF BILL C-57
speechtext: Despicable.

subsubtopic: MOTION RESPECTING ALLOCATION OF TIME FOR REPORT STAGE AND THIRD READING OF BILL C-57
speechtext:
-it is to have that kind of behaviour! One wonders why the national government is held in such contempt by the thousands of people who are attending separatist meetings in western Canada, for example. One wonders why the opposition, in anger, shouts out in this House, delays legislation and so on. This is done in frustration over our inability to perform what we were elected to do, namely, to legislate and to help govern this country. However, that is not the way things are run under this regime. The wisdom comes from the cabinet table and the Privy Council office. Once it arises from that sophisticated process in the Privy Council, and the cabinet decides, that is the end of the matter. We who are nobodies in
Time Allocation
this institution should know better than to try to hope for change and attempt to negotiate change. If we try to talk too long to influence public opinion, the government will use closure to cut us off.
It has been called the five-year dictatorship, and that is what it is. However, in our society, one can only get away with that kind of behaviour for so long. Unless that is recognized soon and some real parliamentary reform changes are brought in to give Parliament some authority, when this group eventually departs it will leave a legacy of a greatly weakened country, weakened national government and weakened institution. If they are honest, they will be able to tell their children and grandchildren that they contributed to the demise of a strong central government in this country. Because that will be the exact consequence of this kind of irresponsible behaviour on the part of the government.
In conclusion, I would simply like to say that what the government has done by this action is to guarantee that a National Energy Program reached by agreement with the negotiating provinces will be that much further delayed. More Canadian money, equipment and people will leave the country, and our likelihood of achieving self-sufficiency will be that much more remote.

Mr. Speaker, today and last week, I listened with a lot of interest to the comments and interventions of members of the opposition from the New Democratic Party, and I would like to recall a few of them because it is very important for the House to understand the problems that they see in our bill. I shall start with the intervention of the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans). He said:
For some time, the government has had a tendency to introduce legislation which would allow it to benefit directly from inflation.
He was talking about the indexing of taxes on alcoholic beverages. However, Mr. Speaker, he completely forgot what we are doing to help individual Canadians. We have indexed personal income tax to make it more equitable and have an income tax system under which all Canadians are treated fairly. The hon. member said nothing about this.
I shall now refer to the hon. member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby). He told us that we have a problem because we need money, and he said the following:
-I have sympathy... for the philosophy espoused by Premier Lougheed in Halifax, Nova Scotia, the other night... The government is not willing to let the economy take its course, and transmit wealth.
And in his speech, he disagreed completely with what we are now doing to share revenue in Canada.

I now turn to what the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) was just saying. He mentioned that this government will be criticized for having done nothing to help create a strong central government. This is fundamental to what we are attempting to do at this time. We are attempting to reduce the

deficit in a measured and even way. We have undertaken measures by which we will begin to bring about a more reasonable sharing of revenues and a more reasonable sharing of equalization throughout all of Canada.
One of the major problems we face deals directly with revenue. The present equalization formula makes no mention of the revenues derived from natural resources; it mentions them only to the extent of 50 per cent. Mr. Speaker, essentially motion No. 6 is a continuation of a great deal of what we have heard in the last number of days with reference to the pricing of wines in an absolute way, the whole matter of indexing, and then the excise tax being placed on wine. In essence, the motion before us does away with the concept of indexing in terms of the excise tax as it applies to wines, and at this point suggests that an increase in the price of Canadian wines is not the appropriate step to take.
Before I discuss some of the details of this motion, I wish to talk about why this particular motion is before us with so many others. Over the last number of days there have been many references to the fact that we were debating 135 different amendments to this particular bill. Members opposite were criticizing us for putting forward so many amendments for discussion. They were asking us why on earth we had not brought in a fewer number of amendments and dealt with more of the specifics and, perhaps, some of the larger issues in this bill.
I want to make it perfectly clear that that is exactly what we had in mind when we deliberately went through second reading stage very quickly in order to get the bill before the committee. I would like to commend the chairman of the finance committee for calling a number of witnesses and for requesting and receiving a number of written briefs. But there was one very important aspect of that deliberation which was eliminated, and that was the opportunity for members of the Conservative party, the Liberal party and the New Democratic Party to come together to discuss what the 23 groups of witnesses presented to us as members of that committee, not to mention countless written breifs which were also presented to us. We eliminated this very crucial step. I suspect that had the government taken that initiative, had it shown that interest, in the next number of days we would not be discussing the vast array of amendments which we are discussing because the matter would have been resolved in committee. Saner heads would have prevailed, in that surely we would have agreed that
the points raised by so many of these delegations and witnesses before the committee were, in fact, legitimate. They expressed legitimate concerns. These were not people trying to avoid paying legitimate taxes to the Government of Canada.
Both opposition parties and members opposite indicated their willingness to ask questions of the witnesses, in terms of finding out what concerns were on their minds. A great many legitimate concerns and criticisms were articulated by the witnesses. Unfortunately, by and large, they were ignored by the government, with the exception of a few cosmetic changes being produced. But the substantive concerns were virtually ignored. That is why members of the Conservative party and ourselves, with a great deal of reluctance, brought in 135 amendments.
We felt the concerns raised by the witnesses were legitimate ones which needed to be addressed. More than ever before I was convinced that this bill is an ad hoc approach to taxation. Attempting to glean a few dollars here and a few dollars there is not the way to approach taxation in Canada in the 1980s. Surely, a reflection of the poor taste and lack of consideration of the government was the document which went to all members of the committee, which attempted to summarize the concerns of the witnesses. Again, as far as the principle is concerned, I commend the chairman of the finance committee for directing his officials to take the time to go through the various briefs, summarize them for us and then provide an appraisal.
Those members who have taken the time to read the appraisal will see that contained therein are comments of the most cynical nature. These were not constructive criticisms, but criticisms designed to make the witnesses appear foolish. These were criticisms designed to make the concerns of the witnesses appear simplistic and almost childish. That is hardly the way to treat serious briefs and presentations in this day and age, particularly when we hear a great deal about the alienation found in certain parts of our country.
When one looks at the various witnesses who appeared before the finance committee, such as representatives of the city of Medicine Hat, representatives of the Hobbema Indian Reserve, the Independent Petroleum Association, the Canadian Petroleum Association, the Federation of Alberta Gas Co-ops, the Energy Services Association of Alberta, and many others, one sees that they were essentially ignored. I do not think there is any question, even from members opposite, about the concerns and points of view which were expressed before the committee being ignored by the government. If that is not a slap in the face to those groups which I have mentioned, in this case westerners, it is little wonder that there exists in our country a cynicism toward the government, an attitude that this government simply does not care. This is why we are being forced to address 135 amendments. The government was not prepared to sit down and discuss ways and means of looking at a few changes to this bill. The government was prepared to simply ignore that process and force the opposition parties into the position of spokesmen for the various witnesses which appeared before the committee.
