The particular motion before us identifies the problem associated with indexation. I do not feel that it is necessary to go through an elaborate and precise description of the hazards associated with indexing the tax on tobacco and alcohol in Canada. The point has been made by many members already that, in fact, this will be a factor which fuels inflation in our country, as opposed to combating it. This measure will give the government a vested interest in inflation, since it is one small step toward providing more revenues for the government as a reflection of inflationary practices. I am concerned about the effect of tying the excise tax to the CPI and what that means as a true reflection of inflation in the country and, therefore, the resultant increase in taxation. For example, if one province decides to increase significantly the price of wine, beer, tobacco or distilled spirits, then that will result in an increase in price across Canada. In other words, one province could dictate a significant increase in the CPI for that subgroup which would then reflect an across-the-board increase for that particular commodity.
If there is a significant increase in the price of a foreign wine or an imported spirit, for example, then it would fuel the CPI for that subgroup, which would result in a rise in prices across Canada. If the value of the Canadian dollar vis-a-vis the franc, or some other currency, drops, the price, if you like, of that imported commodity will increase. It will increase the CPI in that particular subgroup, which will then result in an increase in the price of alcohol and tobacco across the board for all Canadians.
What is happening in this country is that we are tying our increases in the price of alcohol and tobacco to what is happening in foreign countries and to what may be happening in one province of Canada. Surely this is not the intent of this particular piece of legislation. It is with that in mind that we in the New Democratic Party feel that this is simply not the appropriate step to take at all. If it is true, as the hon. member from Ottawa indicated this afternoon, that the need for this is to combat inflation, surely to goodness there is a better way to combat inflation than to index the prices of alcohol and tobacco.
We suggest, when we start looking at the increase in the prices of wine, beer and distilled spirits, that there is a great deal of discrepancy in the pricing of those commodities in Canada today. That is why we have mentioned in our motion that this would appear to be an inappropriate time to add another increase to the price of wine in Canada. We are not against increasing the price of wine; we are against increasing it in this willy-nilly way of adding a few cents to a gallon of wine or a few cents to beer or a few cents to distilled spirits. Surely the reason we are in this disastrous situation today is the kind of ad hoc approach to obtaining federal government revenues.

Mr. Speaker, with the government's amendment to change indexation from a quarterly to an annual basis, I suppose members opposite expect us to get down on our knees with gratitude; that is, having imposed a quarterly system of taxation, the government has now decided to simply do it on an annual basis. I want to tell the minister that once he has accepted the principle that adjustments should only be made on an annual basis, he has eliminated the need for indexation. All the minister has to do is to simply produce the bill in each and every budget, which, one would hope, would be on an annual basis, in order to provide for the increases in taxation which the minister thinks are justified. 1 find it typical of a government which has made a kind of ideological decision to go for indexation on a quarterly basis, every three months, and wants to increase the taxes which the average Canadian would pay in order to have his pint of beer, glass of wine or, indeed, glass of hard liquor, but which now is only going to index on an annual basis, and expects us to be grateful. In fact, the logic that would lead to quarterly adjustments does not apply to the annual adjustments because we have budgets every year so we do not need the indexation.
The second point that has to be made is that the government is kicking Gerald Bouey in the teeth with this proposal, and I think that is a shame. I know the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) thinks it is a shame too because he is behind Governor Bouey 500 per cent. He is "Mr. High Interest" when it comes to bum to bum, toe to toe, cheek to cheek with old Gerry Bouey XVI.
Let us hear what Governor Bouey had to say in his annual report to the Minister of Finance in 1980. What did he have to say about learning to live with inflation? What did he have to say about the principle of indexation? What did he have to say about the principle of providing a free ride to the government and a free ride to the Canadian public? He said, and I am quoting from his annual report:
It is not at all clear what people have in mind when they talk about "learning to live with inflation".
He went on, and I am quoting from pages 5 and 6 of his annual report:
Is it possible that they think that society could develop some way of indexing all money payments so completely that changes in the purchasing power of money would be neutralized and could therefore be ignored in the formation of public policy? The fatal weakness of this idea-
It is fatal. It could kill the government if it adopted this idea. Upon adopting it, the government could die. That is the wording of Governor Bouey.
The fatal weakness of this idea is that the more vigorously a country applied it the more rapidly would any inflationary impetus cause prices to accelerate. That
system would be much too unstable to be workable. As a practical matter proposals to find ways of ignoring the rate of inflation cannot be taken seriously.
That is the view of the Governor of the Bank of Canada about this proposal to index taxation, and I think it is time the government knew it has now broken its commitment to support the Governor of the Bank of Canada in his single-minded policy to fight inflation in Canada. This government is fuelling the fires of inflation. It has broken faith with Gerald Bouey, and I think that is a disgrace.

tobacco, beer, wine and spirits every year. A fantastic concession. He is never going to come back to this House. -the inequity caused by the method chosen as outlined in the most recent amendment would not have been as great.

Now I do not need any member of this House to say to me that the Ontario government has just indexed their taxation in this area. I know they have. Encouraged by the example set by this Minister of Finance, Ontario has done the same thing and the government in Newfoundland has done the same thing. I tell you now that ministers of finance will always take that attitude if they think they can get away with it. Naturally, the poor devils are looking for more revenue and they care not where they get it from.
So this Minister of Finance introduces this inequity into the tax law, this horror, and when the ministers of finance for Ontario and Newfoundland see that he is getting away with it, that he is still alive, that he is not drummed out, that the public have not erupted and got the rope and noose outside the Parliament Buildings to give him a fit reception for such a suggestion, they go ahead and do it themselves. If this House passes these provisions, Mr. Speaker, we will see the eight other provincial finance ministers do the same thing. Believe me, I have some experience. I was minister of finance in Newfoundland and I was minister of finance here for a few brief months, and I know what ministers of finance are like; they have to be watched every minute of the night and day, believe me. So if we do not want this to go through our own House and if we do not want this to become the law in the ten provinces, we have to stop it now before the rot spreads. The MacEachen rot is infecting ministers of finance all across this great dominion.
Now, let us have another look at this indexing provision. The argument has been made that this is fantastic, this is comparable to indexing the personal income tax. That is one of the arguments of some of the Liberal members. Well, Mr. Speaker, one despairs. We have to remember, of course, that the Minister of Finance plans to de-index the personal income tax. He is going to de-index it if he thinks he can get away with it. But I want to tell him now that when he attempts to de-index personal income tax, that is when he is going to be defenestrated, that is when he is no longer going to get away with any tax measures because the unpopularity of that measure is just fantastic. Recent polls to which I have access show that the most unpopular move you can make in the taxation field today in Canada is to de-index the personal income tax. I am giving you a tip, members of the Liberal caucus: stop the Minister of Finance before he attempts to de-index the personal income tax this fall.

HUMAN RIGHTS-AIR CANADA POLICY ON EARLY RETIREMENT OF AIRPLANE PILOTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although I have spoken several times on this particular concern of mandatory retirement, that is, discriminating against and replacing thousands of Canadian "on the shelf' so to speak, I will again ask the government and members of this House to take all possible action to eliminate these policies that are denying our people their right to work and to preserve their healthy self-image.
This discussion today has been stimulated by a question I posed in the House on May 20, 1981, to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) regarding the "dictating" manner in which an airline pilot, Captain Ross Stevenson, is being forced to retire by Air Canada on September 1, 1981.
The Canadian Human Rights Act clearly states in Section 7, that it is a discriminatory practice to directly or indirectly refuse to employ or continue to employ any individual or, in the course of employment, to differentiate adversely in relation to an employee on a prohibited ground of discrimination. Why is Air Canada permitted to use age as a form of discrimination? Is this bureaucratic and mandatory policy not contrary to the principles of the Canadian Human Rights Act?
To further illustrate the point, I draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the double standards that Air Canada is inflicting. Did you know that numerous Canadian airlines operate with pilots who are over 60 years of age, including Nordair, which is owned by Air Canada? Did you know that Air Jamaica operates with pilots over 60 years of age, all the while being managed and operated by Air Canada?
If this is not discriminatory and a policy that goes directly against the grain of our democratic, free and so-called just society, then I do not know what is. Fortunately, I am not alone in this battle to preserve the rights of Canadians by giving them the power to maintain a healthy self-image that many receive from being actively involved in the work force.
As the chairman of the Special Senate Committee stated in the report on retirement age policy entitled "Retirement Without Tears", Senator David Croll emphasized the following:
Adjournment Debate
1.	Progressive abolition of mandatory retirement based on age should become a general policy of the government.
2.	That there should be an increase in the mandatory age of retirement of one year at a time for five years by amending pension plans for retirement rules and conventions. At the end of five years, the concept of compulsory retirement at a particular age would be dropped.
3.	That there should be a review of all human rights legislation because of employee benefits and similar plans.
4.	That there should be created a policy of flexible retirement as the standard for both public and private enterprise.
5.	That there should be amendments to the rules governing public servants and employees of companies under federal jurisdiction, as well as provincial and municipal public servants.
It is here that I would also like to put an abrupt end to the misconception that compulsory retirement is necessary on medical grounds.
Dr. Stanley Mohler, Chief of Flight Applications for the American Federal Aviation Agency, and the Director of Aerospace Medicine at Wright State University in Dayton, Ohio, in the Journal of Aging and Work, states:
The old concepts of pilot aging as a risk factor in flight no longer can be supported, as demonstrated by hard data. The larger, more densely loaded passenger aircraft are flown by the older, more experienced and capable captains, the major factor in today's low accident rate. The rates show that the present age 60 rule is prematurely removing the safest pilots from the air space. Deleting the age 60 rule would, by extrapolation of the accident rate data, further enhance the level of airline flight safety.
Referring back to the reply of the Minister of Transport to my question of May 20, 1981, he stated that these discriminating policies of Air Canada are based on agreements between Air Canada and the Canadian Air Line Pilots Association, CALPA. This is probably correct. However, I do point out that CALPA has at no time conducted a poll or survey of the Air Canada pilots membership to deal specifically with this issue and to determine the wishes of the Air Canada pilots. It is also interesting to note that CALPA has negotiated age 65 retirement for Nordair pilots.
I am not suggesting, as implied by the minister, that government or the Department of Transport go against an agreement reached between an airline and its employees. However, I am advocating that the government, elected by the people, establish the guidelines and laws of this country to eliminate any and all discriminatory practices of mandatory retirement.

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Bockstael (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: HUMAN RIGHTS-AIR CANADA POLICY ON EARLY RETIREMENT OF AIRPLANE PILOTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to preface my remarks on this subject by saying that 1 understand the Canadian Human Rights Commission will be investigating the case referred to by the hon. member. I would not want anything I say to prejudice that investigation, so I will simply state the facts.
As the minister has declared in the House and in correspondence with the hon. member, Transport Canada rules do not require pilots to retire at a specific age. Pilot licences are revalidated after age 60 if the individual successfully meets medical standards. So departmental rules are not at issue here.

June 9, 1981
Adjournment Debate
The retirement age for Air Canada pilots is 60 as a result of an agreement between Air Canada and the Canadian Air Line Pilots Association, referred to as CALPA, the certified bargaining unit for airline pilots.
The hon. member points out that this agreement was reached quite recently, whereas his constituent has been objecting to retirement at age 60 for several years. This may be true, but common labour practice dictates that the agreement should apply to all members of the union indiscriminately. In addition, if the hon. member asks CALPA what its position is, he will find that it has understood retirement at 60 to have been a negotiated feature with the airline since the early 1950s.
It has been suggested that the retirement age at other airlines is 65. This is not exactly the case. The international organization, ICAO, recommends retirement at age 60. For Canadian airlines, the age tends to be 60 as well. There is a small exception for a few Nordair pilots who constitute a very special case. It is my understanding that CALPA would like to standardize age 60 as the requirement age for all airlines for which its member pilots fly.
In these circumstances I think it is clear that it would be quite inappropriate for the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) to intervene in this matter.

Mr. Speaker, on June 4 I directed a question to the Acting Minister of Veterans Affairs. I pointed out to him:
Veterans pension applications, new and appealed, are still not processed and finalized for as long as 62 months, as verified by the Legion. The United States department of veterans affairs takes from 60 to 90 days to finalize an application.

I should like to ask the minister if he will give a firm commitment to the House that he will bring in corrective legislation so that these applications can be processed within 90 days, instead of from one to five years.
The minister answered:
-if any correction can be made in order to improve the disposal of these claims, it will be made. We will do our utmost to improve the system, if it is possible at all, according to the law.
I hope the parliamentary secretary tonight will be informing us that they will be bringing in corrective legislation or, if that is going to cause delays, will bring in an immediate order in council to correct this disgraceful situation that has been taking place in Veterans Affairs.
I should like to put on record tonight the excellent manner in which the United States veterans affairs handles its pension applications.
The aim of the United States department of veterans affairs is to process claims in all stages within 90 days. This would include first-time claims as well as claims for increased benefits. Less than 2 per cent of the claims currently before the U.S. department are six months old. The biggest delay is in obtaining service records and booking medical examination or re-examinations. In spite of this problem, they still process claims in these time frames.
The following is a description of the four basic types of pension claims in the United States. There were over 63,000 applications for compensation for injuries incurred in service, and the average number of days for processing was 137. There were over 25,000 applications for death benefits when death was due to service. These applications took an average of 81 days to process. There were over 87,000 applications based on need. These applications took only 97 days. There were over 107,000 veterans' survivors' pension applications. These took only 65 days to process. In Canada it takes from one to five years. That is a national disgrace.
I have statistics here respecting the death rate among veterans in Canada waiting for their pension applications to be processed. There is no reason for such statistics in the United States.
In the May edition of the Legion magazine there is an editorial about this problem. The editorial points out the following:
In November, 1978, the chairman of the pension commission told a meeting of the standing committee on veterans affairs that the average length of time for a first application to reach a decision was six months, an improvement on the 7.8 months taken earlier. It was, said Allan Solomon, "almost back to normal."
We are nowhere near normal today. There is a continuing controversy over the length of time taken to process applications and the number of applications on hand. This Legion editorial also points out the following:
The number of appeals awaiting consideration by the pension review board hovers around 2,000. Now being heard are applications made two years ago. And the number of new appeals is increasing.
The editorial also says:
By June, 1980, the number of cases awaiting decision had risen from about 2,700 in 1978 to about 4,200. A saving feature, said Mr. Solomon, was a reduction in the number of applications received and "... I think it is a fair assumption to say that in a year's time we should be back to normal."
However, Mr. Solomon admitted in the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs just ten days ago that he is hamstrung by the present legislation and that he cannot process applications any faster. Along with the other two groups which process applications it takes from one to five years. The Auditor General has done an extensive audit of the Department of Veterans Affairs and the time it has taken to process applications. He came up with a figure of 46 months, which is also an absolute disgrace.
June 9, 1981

When dealing with veterans and their pension applications, the Ontario Command of the Royal Canadian Legion writes to veterans and tells them not to expect any action for at least two years. That is an absolute disgrace.
I hope the parliamentary secretary will give us some information tonight, and I hope the government will bring forward new legislation or bring forward an order in council so that the chairman of the pension commission will no longer be hamstrung in dealing with these pension applications and so that we can work toward having a time period similar in length to that in the United States.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Masters (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Mines)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Mines)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in recent days the hon. member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie) has been pressing for a change in the system of processing applications for pensions from veterans and their dependants. I understand his concern about the length of time sometimes taken to adjudicate the applications and, like all of us, I would like to see the adjudication time reduced. However, I would not like to see it reduced at the expense of the veteran. Steps have to be taken to improve the pension system and to curtail the delays in adjudication.
The hon. member has pointed to other countries which provide decisions in less time than is taken by the Canadian system. What he forgets is that the Canadian system was very fully and carefully studied by a commission of inquiry under the chairmanship of Mr. Justice Woods of Saskatchewan, whose report was then fully considered by the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs, which made many recommendations to the government. As a result, the legislation which was then introduced and passed by Parliament was more concerned with safeguarding the claimant and ensuring fair and careful consideration than it was with speed, regardless of outcome.
As an example, hearings before the pension commission or the pension review board are non-adversarial-no one appears to suggest an award should not be made: The only advocates present at a hearing represent the claimants. The speed with which a decision is made is not a measure of its quality.
The veterans organizations have consistently supported the commission in its view that speed was secondary to good and beneficial decisions. The proof of the wisdom of this attitude is that prior to the Woods committee report upon which much of the current legislation is based, only 20 per cent of all applications were granted at the first level. In the last ten years it has averaged 41 per cent, this despite the fact that the simple claims of gunshot wounds and the like were long since granted and that today's claims, which in the main deal with problems of aging, are much more difficult to relate to a period of military service. If careful research into the background and facts of the claims were not undertaken, there would be many more negative decisions.
In some other countries pension claims are handled with greater speed, but our system is different in both essence and
Adjournment Debate
approach. Our legislation instructs the commission to collect relevant material and to make inquiries into the facts. The thoroughness with which this is done accounts for some of the delay factors. The Auditor General's recent report indicated that in some cases it can take up to 46 months from the time of an original application until a claim is considered at final appeal. The report, however, does acknowledge that much of this delay is outside the control of the pension commission or the pension review board in that there are periods when they may not proceed until such time as they receive agreement of the applicant, which in some cases may take weeks or months or even years.
The pension commission and the pension review board are doing their utmost to reduce the time taken for decisions to be rendered. Although it is easy to give a negative decision, they will not do so for the sake of speed to the detriment of the veterans and their dependants.
Let them die!

GRAIN-COMPENSATION TO FARMERS FOR EMBARGO ON SHIPMENTS TO RUSSIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise this evening to participate in the adjournment debate and refer to a question that I had the opportunity to put to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on June 2, concerning the long overdue grain compensation payments to Canadian producers as a result of the embargo imposed upon the shipment of grain to Russia after it raided Afghanistan. I do not want to get into why there should or should not be payments forthcoming to grain producers in Canada; I think the principle is well established and well accepted. It was accepted by the Clark government right after the invasion in January of 1980. Subsequent to that, during the election campaign and right after it the Prime Minister promised to abide by the decision of the Clark government to see that grain producers were not left to bear the full burden of foreign policy as it was pursued by the whole country. That was a promise made by this government some 15 or 16 months ago.
There was some concern at that time as to how the level of compensation was to be arrived at. Since that time a study was done by the Parliamentary Library that came up with a figure. As far back as July 22, the University of Saskatchewan released a study, and I quote from the Brandon Sun which says:
Prairie farmers have lost $62.5 million because of Canada's support of the U.S.-led grain embargo against the Soviet Union, agricultural economists at the University of Saskatchewan estimate.
That is July 22, 1980, which is some 11 months ago. Subsequent to that, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) said that there would be a statement by August 1, 1980, as to what the level of compensation payments would be. Prior to that there were statements made that an amount should be determined before the end of the crop year. Anyone connected with western agriculture knows that the crop year in this country runs from August 1 to July 31. So if we took the

June 9, 1981
Adjournment Debate
Minister of Agriculture at his word when he said it was going to be by August 1, or by the end of the crop year in 1980, it meant that ten months has gone by since that commitment was made.
Subsequently, the Minister of Agriculture said that payments would be made in November, 1980. Obviously the government is delaying its decision.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) also promised that payments would be made in November, 1980. As far back as October, 1980, the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board, Senator Argue, who does not sit in this place and cannot answer our questions during Question Period, said that payments would be made in January, 1981. Senator Argue cannot really be accountable to those of us who are elected by grain producers in the country. In December 1980, the Minister of Agriculture said that the final report on payments had yet to be submitted to cabinet for a decision but that he hoped this would take place within a few days. Again this was five months ago.
In January, 1981, Senator Argue said that payments would be made in January, 1981. Again the government procrastinated. In February, 1981, the Prime Minister said that officials from various government departments were establishing the damages and would finish their work very soon. In March, 1981, the Minister of Agriculture said he would soon know the amount. Two months ago, in April, 1981, the Minister of Agriculture told Parliament that the payments would be announced in a few days.
I could go on, but the process 1 think, is becoming rather sickening for those of us who represent agricultural communities and agricultural constituencies. It is rather sickening to see how the government has delayed in making this announcement. It has been well over a year-and perhaps closer to 15 months-since the original commitment was made by the government. Since then nothing has happened.
I should like to suggest two things. First, there is no doubt that the principle has been accepted by the government. This was confirmed by the Prime Minister on June 2. If the problem in so far as the government is concerned is the amount, I suggest that it make an initial payment on the compensation so that producers, who are very much in need of funds because of high interest rates and other expenses incurred in putting their crops in the ground, could at least have access to the payment and know that the government was talking in good faith when it said that it would honour the commitment of the Clark government. The government should make an interim payment and then determine what the full amount should be.
Second, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) castigates the opposition for asking for increased government expenditures and at the same time saying that we want to reduce the deficit. If they have any decency, presumably they would have allowed for some expenditures to make payments to farmers as a result of the embargo. They would have allowed
for that in the estimates and that money would have been forthcoming. This would have been one way to alleviate some of the problems associated with high interest rates without adding to the government deficit.
I should like to close by reading part of an editorial which appeared in the Brandon Sun on June 4, 1981. The last paragraph of the article sums up the attitude of many westerners toward the government. It reads:
The Trudeau government has dawdled long enough on the embargo payments. Westerners are not going to forget the debt. More delays will only confirm what many westerners already believe: with the Trudeau government, the needs of the west come last.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Ostiguy) is here tonight. I hope he can make some meaningful announcement after 15 months of intolerable delay. It is a very shameful treatment of a very important sector of the Canadian economy. I hope the parliamentary secretary can do something by making an announcement which would give us some faith in the government keeping its word to Canadian grain producers.

Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member for Portage-Marquette (Mr. Mayer) mentioned a few moments ago, it was after the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan that the United States announced that they were taking sanctions against the Soviet Union. The American government contacted other exporting countries and it was at that time that Canada agreed to restrict its grain exports to the U.S.S.R. The Canadian government of the day, under Mr. Clark, as the hon. member for Portage-Marquette indicated, agreed to subsidize grain farmers and promised to compensate them for the losses sustained because of the embargo. The present government agreed to live up to those commitments and to compensate grain producers for their losses related to the government's decision to restrict grain shipments to the U.S.S.R. But precisely as a result of this embargo, surpluses have accumulated both in Canada and in the U.S. as well as in other countries, and as a result, prices have dropped. However, this was partly offset by the American government's decision to withdraw from the market part of the grain by instructing the Commodity Credit Corporation to buy grain and by stocking more grain than provided for under the agricultural reserves program. Pursuant to its commitment to grain producers, the Canadian government had instructed an interdepartmental committee to look into the matter and come up with a compensation system and to determine how much was to be paid and how the payments were to be made.
At the same time, a number of organizations and institutions have assessed the losses suffered by our grain producers. The board has taken more time than expected to look into the estimations, and most of the data needed for the analysis were not available. It is a fact that when the prices dropped and the

embargo was imposed on Russia, it made quite a difference. Then, there was the increase in interest rates.
